newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Polish deputy PM says not worried by zloty trend.
newsitem.headline: Polish deputy PM says not worried by zloty trend.

text.p: Polish Deputy Prime Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday he was not concerned about a recent weakening of the zloty and said the central bank was in control of the situation.

The zloty eased on Wednesday to its lowest level since May against its currency basket. Dealers say the zloty has been under downward pressure from foreign investors who were trimming portfolios amid rising interest rates and concerns over external imbalances.
Belka, who is also Finance Minister, told reporters the central bank, concerned about the trade deficit, was accepting a certain weakening of the zloty within its fluctiation band against the basket.
"This is clearly something that does not worry us at all. The trend is in the direction we wish to have and the central bank is very much in control," he said.

The zloty is gradually devalued in a crawling peg system. The monthly devaluation rate has been one percent since the beginning of the year but Belka said the authorities were starting to think of decelerating the slide.

A deputy president of the national bank was quoted last month as saying Poland could face a Czech-style financial crisis and a gaping current account deficit, stemmimg from a wide trade gap, next year unless it balanced its 1998 budget.
But Belka, whose ministry wants to cut the budget deficit next year to 1.9 percent of GDP from 2.8 percent, said the planned fiscal adjustment should be enough to keep the trade gap stable.
"I think it is enough to stabilise the trade deficit which we in the government and the national bank consider fully manageable and posing no danger to the reserves and to the zloty," he said.
After the first four months of this year, the trade gap was $4 billion, twice as much as in the same period of 1996.
The central bank says Poland can only afford a budget deficit fo 1.5 percent of GDP next year and should aim for a balanced budget as soon as possible.
"If we see the trade deficit widening, then we will go for entire budget balancing but I don't think we have to plan now and say that in two years we will will balance the budget," he said.

Belka said the annual inflation rate in June was likely to be 14.6-15 percent, compared with 14.6 percent in May. He said "crazy" movements in food prices made it difficult to estimate June inflation.
"In July we will have a fall in inflation far bigger than last year, so we will come back to May or much below it. I am not at all worried by June."
